message.content:
Sure! Those numbers are already a pair of geographic coordinates (latitude = 37.4224764, longitude = ‑122.0842499). If you’d like to see what real‑world place they point to, you can feed them into Google’s Geocoding API (or any other reverse‑geocoding service) to get an address, place name, or additional metadata.

Here’s a quick example of how you could call the Google Geocoding API from your own code:

```python
import requests

lat = 37.4224764
lng = -122.0842499
api_key = "YOUR_API_KEY"   # <-- replace this with your actual key

url = f"https://maps.googleapis.com/maps/api/geocode/json?latlng={lat},{lng}&key={api_key}"
response = requests.get(url)
data = response.json()

if data["status"] == "OK":
    print("Formatted address:", data["results"][0]["formatted_address"])
else:
    print("Error:", data["status"])
```

If you run that snippet with a valid API key, you’ll get something like:

```
Formatted address: 1600 Amphitheatre Parkway, Mountain View, CA 94043, USA
```

That tells you the coordinates point to Google’s headquarters in Mountain View, California.

---

### Quick “no‑code” way

If you don’t want to write code, just paste the URL into a browser (replace `YOUR_API_KEY` with a real key):

```
https://maps.googleapis.com/maps/api/geocode/json?latlng=37.4224764,-122.0842499&key=YOUR_API_KEY
```

The JSON response will contain the same information as above.

---

**What if you’re looking for the *reverse*—i.e., turning an address into coordinates?**

Just swap the query parameters:

```
https://maps.googleapis.com/maps/api/geocode/json?address=1600+Amphitheatre+Parkway,+Mountain+View,+CA+94043&key=YOUR_API_KEY
```

That will return the latitude/longitude pair you started with (plus any other details).
